💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 07:10 EST, 20 November 2026.
  • While thinking over the last few days about his first press conference as Manchester United boss, Mauricio Pochettino would not have expected drones and the fresh Grand Theft Auto video game to be top of the agenda.
  • Having touched down in Manchester on Wednesday, taking a private jet laid on by United in the immediate aftermath of the United States’ game in Cincinnati against Haiti, it has been a whirlwind 48 hours for Pochettino and his staff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 07:00 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 07:10 EST, 20 November 2026.

While thinking over the last few days about his first press conference as Manchester United boss, Mauricio Pochettino would not have expected drones and the fresh Grand Theft Auto video game to be top of the agenda.

Having touched down in Manchester on Wednesday, taking a private jet laid on by United in the immediate aftermath of the United States’ game in Cincinnati against Haiti, it has been a whirlwind 48 hours for Pochettino and his staff.

On Thursday, he took charge of training for the first time against the backdrop of question marks around Bryan Mbeumo’s decision to post late into the night about popular new video game GTA VI.

By the time the day ended, the glitch at hand was far more pressing as a drone pilot filmed and uploaded to YouTube a 12-minute video from Pochettino’s first session at Carrington.

How worried Pochettino actually is about the footage – which has since been pulled from YouTube, with a grovelling apology issued – remains to be seen but only this summer did the Argentine concede that ‘we are in an era of spies’.

The footage wasn’t a tactical golden ticket for Liverpool, but what was there to take from it?

A drone pilot filmed and uploaded to YouTube a 12-minute video from Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session as Manchester United manager.

The players get to work, with United's coaching staff seemingly unaware that their every move is being followed from the skies.

Pochettino sides have had a consistent set-up with and without the ball over the years.

The Argentine and his staff have, more often than not, leaned into a back-three in possession, shifting to a back-four without the ball.

In the drone footage we could see the United squad divided into three groups with one XI out on a different training pitch with Pochettino and coach Toni Jimenez.

That group were lined up in what appeared to be that preferred in-possession set-up, with academy defender Reece Munro tucking in from right back to form a back-three alongside Harry Maguire and Ayden Heaven, traditional centre backs in a back-four.

Pochettino likes to have at least one full back push on extremely high to provide the width and in this snippet of his first training session, that responsibility landed on the shoulders of teenager Harry Amass, who has struggled for minutes this season, getting a total of just 29 under Michael Carrick.

The United players are put into position by Pochettino at Carrington.

Recent findings suggest that similarly, Pochettino has often shown a desire to play No 10s – or attacking midfielders – quite narrow. And that is what we saw here, with Amass and Mbeumo providing the width. Mbeumo was on the right of a 4-2-3-1 shape with Matheus Cunha and 17-year-old academy talent Jaume Camacho playing narrower and Joshua Zirkzee up front.

The formation becomes a 3-2-4-1 in possession with the full back pushing on to the wing, creating two No 10s behind the lone striker.

The footage was significant in that it showed Pochettino is implementing his ideas from day one and is wasting no time in trying to embed a style he needs players to get up to speed with rapidly.

But little should be read into the personnel given it was an amalgamation of young players and senior regulars.

We could see academy players Amass, Camacho and Munro among the 10 outfield players, along with Cunha, Heaven, Maguire, Kobbie Mainoo, Mbeumo, Andrey Santos and Zirkzee.

Of the 10 that were put to task by Pochettino, only four have started more than five league games this season.

It is highly improbable that the personnel used will be anywhere close to the starting XI at Anfield on Sunday.

The footage also demonstrated games of one-touch rondos going on between the two other groups which were divided between the rest of Pochettino’s coaching team, which includes his son Sebastiano and Miguel D’Agostino, as well as trusted assistant Jesus Perez.

Pochettino greets his newly introduced players including Bryan Mbeumo, who lined up out wide in the first training session.

United's players start a 'rondo', where one defender stands in the middle and tries to pinch the ball from the players stood around the edge - who are allowed one touch at a time.

One group included Diogo Dalot, Leny Yoro, Lisandro Martinez, Matthijs de Ligt, Youri Tielemans, Mason Mount and Noussair Mazraoui. The other was academy-led with Bruno Fernandes leading a rondo that featured Shea Lacey, Jack and Tyler Fletcher, Dan Armer, as well as Jaydan Kamason.

But the use of Mbeumo in Pochettino’s work was one of the most interesting aspects, largely because he was back operating in a wider role.

Sources indicate that with injuries hampering Benjamin Sesko, Mbeumo has had to spend a lot of the season deployed through the middle. That could well have to continue given Sesko is not anticipated to return until late January, but Pochettino’s decision to use Zirkzee as the figurehead in his set-up was intriguing.

Pochettino’s principles and set-up won’t vary too much; the onus now is on players to adapt. But Pochettino and Jimenez did look to have players in the correct positions. There were no obvious experiments – which makes sense when time is of the essence.

Amass plays off the left, Munro is a centre back, Maguire is comfortable in the middle of any back three, Camacho plays as a No 10 in the academy, both Mainoo and Santos have played together in a double pivot at the base of midfield and Zirkzee is a centre forward.

Pochettino likes a centre forward who can drop in to allow No 10s to run beyond and that suits Zirkzee’s style well, allowing him to be involved as a link man and not isolated with his back to goal.

Mbeumo works better running in behind as a counter-attacking striker, playing on the shoulder of the last defender.

How Pochettino uses Mbeumo over the longer term remains curious because swap out Camacho for Fernandes and Amass for Dorgu and there is a plausible set-up for success, with Mbeumo holding width on the right, Cunha and Fernandes in those central pockets they crave most, and Dorgu holding width off the left.

Lisandro Martinez (left) and Leny Yoro also meet Pochettino and his staff at Carrington.

Pochettino’s track record of working with and improving young players became immediately apparent, with so many given an introduction to his staff and their methods on day one.

While both Jack and Tyler Fletcher, along with Amass, Lacey and Bendito Mantato have made their first-team debuts, it was a golden opportunity in particular for Camacho, the stand-out player in the academy this season following the exit of JJ Gabriel.

United routinely promote multiple academy players each day to bolster numbers in first-team training sessions and it’s a good way for staff to bridge the gap in speed, physicality and intensity between senior and youth football.

Every manager that comes in likes to take on a project and when Ruben Amorim walked through the door it was Godwill Kukonki that caught the eye of staff.

Gabriel became a training mainstay in the months prior to his bombshell request to terminate his contract, and now Camacho, Munro and Armer are working towards first-team debuts instead.

#1568. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

📅 20 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals.
  • What makes a good player great, and a great player the best?
  • After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals.

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

It has been revealed that based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Sources indicate that those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

According to recent reports, one lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Recent findings suggest that around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

It has been revealed that C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

According to recent reports, but the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

In a recent development, there is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s blueprint was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

Jude Bellingham scored twice in Miami as England came from behind to end Norway’s sensational World Cup run back in July.

But Erling Haaland’s team will be out for revenge after their incredible comeback to beat Denmark secured progress to the two-legged Nations League quarter-finals.

Recent findings suggest that the Republic of Ireland face a tough test against Croatia as they attempt to reach League A for the first time. Both ties will be played across two legs, also in March.

Norway will be out for revenge against England, who could face Jurgen Klopp’s Germany if they reach the semi-finals.

England have been handed a suspended ban for away supporters as a result of “racist and/or discriminatory behaviour” by fans during Sunday’s 3-2 win over Spain in Madrid.

The ban, which would apply to one match, is suspended for a period of two years, meaning any similar offence during that period would enforce it.

The FA has also been fined €15,000 (£12,600).

The four Nations League quarter-finals will be played across two legs during the international break in March 2027.

The first legs will be played over the 25-27th March with the second legs played between 28-30th March.

The semi-finals and final will follow in June 2027 following the end of the 2026/27 domestic season.

Jurgen Klopp must be feeling confident about Germany’s chances of progressing further in the competition.

The German team haven’t been anywhere near their best so far but they’re drawn against an aging and rebuilding Beglium team in the quarter-finals.

Belgium managed to come through a pressure-filled contest against Italy in the group stage in a sign of their lasting quality but Germany will be favourites.

The Germans also have the added motivation of a possible semi-final with England to come so they should be firing on all cylinders come the quarter-finals in March.

In the third quarter-final the Netherlands will host Portugal.

Portugal have very fond memories of the Nations League having won the competition twice including the inaugural tournament.

They are also the reigning champions having beaten Spain in a penalty shootout last year.

Can the Netherlands muster up enough quality to overcome a Cristiano Ronaldo-less Portugal side and reach the final four?

Elsewhere the Nations League quarter-finals have also thrown up another World Cup rematch.

This one is from the semi-finals as Spain take on France once again.

Spain have won each of the last three knockout games against France with those coming in three different competitions.

They won 2-1 in the Euro 2024 semi-finals before a 5-4 victory in the Nations League semi-finals in 2025.

Most recently, of course, they won 2-0 in the World Cup semi-finals in a match they completely dominated.

Can France overcome them across two legs this time around?

England’s quarter-final tie against Norway will be a rematch of their meeting at this summer’s World Cup.

The Three Lions triumphed on that occasion with Jude Bellingham scoring twice to overturn Andreas Schjelderup’s opener and secure a 2-1 win after extra-time.

Norway were arguably the better team on the day though and will feel confident about challenging England over two-legs come March.

What does that mean for England?

Thomas Tuchel’s men will take on Norway in the quarter-finals.

Should they progress from that tie they will face either Germany or Belgium in the semi-finals.

If they reach the final they will play one of France, Spain, Portugal or the Netherlands.

Now, a draw is made to determine the semi-final fixtures.

In the first semi-final will be the winners of quarter-final three.

They will take on the winners of quarter-final one.

In the second semi-final the winners of quarter-final four will face the winners of two.

Latest Update: Czechia braces for massive protest against public media reform plans

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

In a recent development, the right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that presently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

The parties argue that the latest arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism.".

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has mentioned that a fresh proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country.".

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," mentioned Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation.".

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Matthew Briggs became an instant pub quiz question in his very fist game in senior football.

By coming off the bench against Middlesbrough in May 2007, the Fulham left-back set a upcoming Premier League record as its youngest-ever player.

Briggs inherited the distinction from Izzy Brown and would give it up to Harvey Elliott 12 years later, before Ethan Nwaneri set the mark at 15 years, 181 days in 2022.

But as Briggs told FourFourTwo: "Being the Premier League’s youngest player was one of the greatest moments and achievements of my life, but it came with a lot of pressure.

"When I eventually lost the title to Harvey Elliott after 12 long years - the longest anyone has had it - it felt like the pressure had been lifted and I could just be me.

"People had always been wondering why I wasn’t doing this and that, why I wasn’t achieving what they believed I should have been achieving.

"It’s a lot of noise to deal with. I have sympathy for Harvey Elliott now, too.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

I actually thought he was doing well at Liverpool, and he’s still young enough to get back to doing what he does best.".

Briggs believes that starting at such a high level so young can make the adaptation that much harder if you end up having to work your way back up the pyramid.

That's particularly true if your first move away comes as abruptly as it did for Briggs when he left Fulham for Millwall in 2014in the first permanent switch of his itinerant career.

Briggs explained: "I suffered a lot of injuries, although I was offered a three-year contract extension before I left Fulham.

"But Martin Jol got sacked, a newly introduced manager came in and got rid of the whole team – I was injured at the time, and he wanted to bring in fresh blood. I’d been there since the age of 10.

"When you drop down the leagues, you have the aspiration to get back to the top, but when you get to a certain age, it’s harder to do that, especially when you’re suffering with injuries.

In a recent development, "I suffered a lot with mental health because of that. Everything that was my superpower – speed, power, getting up and down the pitch, my body was stopping me from doing it.

Recent findings suggest that "I went to Denmark and really enjoyed my first season, but then my hip started playing up again and they told me I should retire, because I had no cartilage in my hip. I came back to the UK and played non-league for two more years, but my body just gave up.".

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Working on one of the world's biggest football video games is the perfect combination of my two biggest passions, gaming and football.

I'm CJ Ramson. I work on the creation of football video games. I work on Football Manager as an associate QA manager. QA stands for quality assurance.

According to recent reports, we're the ones that test the game. We make sure everything works, and we work closely with the developers to try and make the most realistic simulation of football.

Sources indicate that growing up, I loved football, whether that was playing football or playing football video games with my friends. I'd always be doing one or the other. With the video games, the thing that really drew me to them was I've always been into the tactical side of the game, either being able to control the players or create your own tactics.

So a typical day for us, we'll get a fresh build in from the developers. We'll test it as a QA team, and we'll look for either bugsor ways that we can improve the game. That can be anything from the runs that players make, to decisions they make on the ball, what the team instructions and tactics do. So there's a lot of areas for us to cover. Our final goal is to make it as realistic to real football as possible.

So even though my background was in coaching, there was a lot of transferable skills that I learned and developed through my time coaching that I managed to transfer into this. So whether that's being really analytical and having a good eye for detail and knowingwhen to pick things out and what to look for, or it could be things like timekeeping and making sure things run perfectly on time, and working with other people as well. So social skills where you have to work within a team or even lead a team.

The animation he makes, and the ball physics as well, where the ball goes off after the save.".

So as much as I loved playing football, I realised quite early on I probably wasn't going to be a professionalfootballer. But I wanted to work in football and find. So at college, I studied sports science, and that's where I found my love of coaching. I did my FA Level 1 and then went on to do my FA Level 2. After I left college, I got a job at Arsenal, which was unpaid, working with them, learning how to develop my coaching skills. Which then led to me having a full-time paid job at Fulham Football Club, working with the youth teams, working with the academy teams. And then that eventually led to me going to an event. I saw an opportunity where you could apply for a job in Football Manager. It was something that naturally I was interested in, had a conversation with them, and realised it was definitely something that I would love to do.

So I went to the networking event at Kick It Out, and that was an opportunity for me to network with other football coaches, other people within the gaming industries, and have a really good insight to different jobs in football gaming. Without doing that, I wouldn't have the opportunity to meet the people at Football Manager and see a upcoming job in gaming, which I wouldn't have beenaware of.

Sources indicate that one of the highlights of my career so far is working on the in-and-out-of-possession system on FM 26. This is something we see in real football all the time, so being part of the team that brought that to life and brought it into the game was super cool.

In a recent development, working within the football industry is a dream come true. Being able to work on something that I'm passionate about, that is played and enjoyed by millions of people, is an amazing feeling for me and an amazing opportunity that I have. And yeah, I love it.

To find out what other jobs you could have in football, explore the BBC Bitesize Follow Your Passion collection.

Ever wondered who makes sure your video games are great? This guy!

CJ works as an associate quality assurance manager on the video game Football Manager. His team test the game to make sure everything works, and collaborate with the developers to create the most realistic simulation of football.

There are lots of different ways to progress in the gaming industry.

In a recent development, CJ works in the QA (Quality Assurance) team, testing games. In this team, his career progression has followed this path:.

QA tester --> QA lead --> QA manager.

His team is just one of the options, though. "There are lots of other roles within the industry too, including production, game design, social media and development, where developers help to code the game," he explains. "Depending on your skills and interests, there are different pathways you can take that you might enjoy and be suited to.".

There are different roles in video game testing. CJ notes that: "Salaries can vary depending on your role and the manufacturer you work for. They can range from around Â£20,000 to Â£50,000 and upwards." The higher salaries in this range could apply when you've gained more experienced and progressed in your career.

CJ is now a quality assurance manager, but he started out as a quality assurance tester. Find out more about the role of QA tester below. This role can have various other job titles, such as games tester, computer games tester, and video games tester.

You could get into this role via a university course, a college course (such as a Level 3 Diploma in Creative Media, an A-level in Computing, or a T-level in Digital Software Development (England only)), an apprenticeship, or applying directly if you have relevant experience.

This information is a guide and is constantly changing. Please check the National Careers Service website for the latest information and all the qualifications needed and the GOV.UK website for more on T-levels.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Below, you can review our collection of news and analysis on stories from or relating to Germany from Friday, November 13.
  • According to recent reports, german Chancellor Friedrich Merz got a birthday cake at the UN climate summit in Turkey this week.
  • According to recent reports, fridays for Future is taking its demands to German streets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These updates have been closed. Below, you can review our collection of news and analysis on stories from or relating to Germany from Friday, November 13.

According to recent reports, german Chancellor Friedrich Merz got a birthday cake at the UN climate summit in Turkey this week. But he wasn't there to eat it. Meanwhile, in Berlin, climate activists marked his 71st birthday on Friday with a symbolic chocolate cake. Their message: they too want to reach that age on a livable planet.

According to recent reports, fridays for Future is taking its demands to German streets. Demonstrations were planned in more than 70 German cities on Friday, November 13.

Under the slogan "Pay your climate debt," protesters in the German capital demanded more funding for climate protection and adaptation in developing countries, alongside a global phase-out of coal, oil and gas.

Germany provided €4.7 billion ($5.2 billion) in federal budget funds for international climate financing in 2025 — below its €6 billion pledge.

But the protest movement is no longer drawing the crowds it once did. In September 2019, Fridays for Future mobilized an estimated 1.4 million people across Germany. Five years later, that figure fell to around 75,000 at a comparable nationwide strike.

This comes as broader youth frustration with German politics grows. "I don't feel addressed by the chancellor unfortunately," Kim, a protester in Berlin, told DW.

From military service to affordable housing and climate policy, younger Germans are questioning whether their concerns are being heard.

A recent nationwide poll found that 82% of Germans believe politicians do not adequately represent young people's interests. Among 18- to 34-year-olds, just 5% trust Merz's conservatives to champion their concerns, compared with 3% for their Social Democratic coalition partners.

According to recent reports, merz is not the first German chancellor to miss a UN climate summit. And smaller demonstrations do not necessarily mean young Germans care less about climate change. But the contrast is striking: while the climate movement struggles to mobilize, dissatisfaction among younger voters extends well beyond environmental policy.

Julian Reichelt, formerly the editor-in-chief of Germany's top-selling tabloid Bild, indicates he was the target of an arson attack after his car was set on fire and largely destroyed in Berlin.

Now editor-in-chief of the right-wing online portal Nius that he co-founded, Reichelt said the arson attack took place in the Charlottenburg district of the German capital overnight.

Recent findings suggest that police confirmed the car was intentionally set alight, saying a passerby reported it shortly after 2 a.m. that morning. However, they did not name a suspect or potential personal motive at first, saying only that the fire department responded and extinguished the fire.

"It is completely clear that this was a targeted attack," Reichelt said, calling it an "attempt at intimidation against new free media that stand up against this left-wing extremism.".

Similar arson attacks several years ago targeted cars belonging to a columnist for another Berlin newspaper, B.Z., with a left-wing group claiming responsibility in one case.

Recent findings suggest that that noted, Berlin also has a more general and fairly well documented problem with arson and vandalism targeting cars, with an average of roughly two a night being set alight in the capital city over recent years. Vandalism and insurance fraud are the most common reasons more generally.

Reichelt was fired from his prominent job at Bild in 2021 amid allegations of sexual harassment, accusations he always denied and referred to as a "smear campaign.".

Lawmakers in the Bundestag have approved reforms that will provide additional powers to Germany's domestic and external intelligence agencies.

The changes will strengthen both the external Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and domestic intelligence service the BfV, formally titled the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.

The law passed fairly comfortably in the federal Bundestag lower house of parliament, with 309 votes in favor, 190 against and 71 abstentions.

The BfV will be granted powers beyond intelligence gathering and monitoring individuals, such as being able to secretly enter homes or take action against explosives or weapons.

In the case of the BND, it will be granted additional operational intervention powers, for instance moving to disable servers belonging to state-sponsored hacker groups abroad.

The changes aim to respond to intensified and evolving threats from foreign intelligence services and their partners, and to reduce dependency on information supplied by friendly foreign intelligence services.

Opposition parties have accused the government of abolishing or weakening the separation between the police and intelligence services — a sensitive and closely monitored distinction in German society, because of the legacy both of Adolf Hitler's Nazi regime and of the secret police services in Communist East Germany during the Cold War.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Friedrich Merz has stated during his visit to Dublin that Germany and Europe's position in future peace talks for Ukraine is "set.".

Following the talks in Abu Dhabi this week between Ukraine and Russia brokered by the US, which also involved European representatives at times, Merz said further negotiations were now planned.

"In the coming weeks there should now be concrete peace talks in which Europe is represented," Merz told reporters in Dublin amid an informal meeting of EU leaders.

He said that "provisionally" this might involve the same "group of Europeans" who had participated in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday.

"Germany is set in there, that is completely clear," he said.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's call to link EU budget negotiations to the provision of assistance to Ukraine, which faced hefty criticism at home, has found some backing amid European Political Community meetings and an AI summit in Dublin.

Merz, who has been leading the charge to find savings in the next EU budget, remarked doing so could ensure stronger contributions to helping Ukraine from all EU member states.

Estonia's Prime Minister Kristen Michal said during the meeting in Dublin that he approved of Merz's suggestion "that support for Ukraine is also a part of our core security and our core financing.".

He remarked that members who wanted a newly introduced EU budget should contribute.

Latvia's Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, meanwhile, mentioned he agreed completely with Merz.

According to recent reports, "We must all pull in the same direction. All of Europe must do its part," he mentioned.

Luxembourg's Luc Frieden also remarked that "we must all stand behind Ukraine" and added that collective financial commitments should be a part of this.

As the largest economy and most populous country in the EU, Germany is the largest overall contributor both to the EU budget and to assistance for Ukraine.

Countries that tend to be so-called net beneficiaries of the EU budget, rather than net contributors to it, tend to be more reticent to cut spending plans.

Hosts Ireland, in a tricky position as the holders of the rotating presidency of the EU trying to broker a deal on the next seven-year budget, remarked it had concerns about adding an additional factor to the stalled talks, as the current budget's expiry at the end of 2027 starts to draw near.

"But I do understand why this is happening," Taoiseach (or prime minister) Micheal Martin mentioned in Dublin. "Some countries have made considerable contributions and they want all EU member states to contribute financially to the support for Ukraine.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) was critical of both the spending and the fundraising prepares in the 2027 budget, claiming without showing its workings that it would be able to do more with less by making swingeing cuts in various key areas.

Budget policy spokesman Michael Espendiller remarked the budget meant "more debts and more taxes and more burdens for the taxpayer.".

He accused the Christian Democrats of breaking key election pledges by raising taxes on alcohol and tobacco. He then complained that despite this, there was not enough money for the promised electricity tax cut.

"If you put it into figures, the federal government will be taking out almost €400,000 (around $440,000) every minute in new debt," Espendiller said, calling for an end to what he called a spiral of debt.

He claimed that the AfD would have able to complete its budget with latest debt of just €63 billion, not roughly €210 billion, while simultaneously providing tax relief of around €44 billion.

Espendiller mentioned this would be achieved with wide-reaching cuts in several core areas of spending: climate protection, contributing to the EU budget and other EU funding, asylum-related spending, international development aid, and weapons deliveries and other assistance to Ukraine.

It's unclear to what extent these proposed cuts would be feasible or legal, or what domestic or international implications they might have, or whether they'd save anything like the amount the AfD asserts in practice.

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

The session took over 15 hours, and already politicians are talking about areas where they still see room for further improvement or alteration — but the document does at least stand in such a form in which it can take effect without too many complications.

Including all spending plans, in the core budget and from the so-called "special funds" for infrastructure and military modernization, fresh debt constitutes around a third of oultays.

In total, the plan is to take out newly introduced debt worth just over €210 billion ($233 billion), while taking in a little less than €400 billion in taxes.

Industry observers note that that's the second-highest level of new debt in the post-war history of the Federal Republic of Germany. Even at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021, new debt was only slightly higher, at €215.4 billion.

We'll likely be returning to the various details of and reactions to this story throughout the morning.

The environmentalist Greens took aim at Chancellor Merz for not delivering on a promise to reduce taxes on electricity in the final budget.

"The significant promise that Chancellor Merz made a few days ago, sinking electricity taxes for everyone, this promise remains a broken promise," party co-leader Britta Hasselmann noted on ZDF television on Friday.

"It was possible to find a way at short notice for several other things in this budget," she remarked.

"I think this demonstrates the inadequate planning and the weak leadership of the chancellor," Hasselmann mentioned.

She added that the CDU forcing a delay to the planned sugar tax at short notice was further evidence of the planning shortcomings.

A budget expert at the party, Sebastian Schäfer, similarly alleged a "leadership vacuum in this coalition government," saying that what was put forward was less a budget and more a "wooden shack wihtout foundations.".

The Left Party's budget policy spokesman Dietmar Bartsch has lamented a "knot garden of debt, tricks and delays," accusing the coalition of not conducting "responsible budgetary policy.".

Despite criticizing the debt levels, Bartsch also mentioned it was "deeply unserious" to float electricity tax relief but then withdraw the blueprint.

He said this would have cost less money than the federal government's plan to buy a share of the arms firm KNDS. He also said it was unacceptable for the center-left Social Democrats to be celebrating just because "the odd welfare cut is not happening.".

Ines Schwerdtner, co-leader of the party that firmly opposes defense spending and is at best lukewarm on NATO membership, mentioned the record spending indicated that money was not as tight as Merz's government made out.

"The debt brake is suspended for weapons, but for housing and electricity taxes they scrimp for every euro," Schwerdtner said. "The money is there, this government is just distributing it completely incorrectly.".

Schwerdtner, herself a member of the budget committed in the Bundestag, called it a "budget of naivete.".

More on this morning's top story in Berlin, the 2027 budget being signed off.

As the CDU calls for further savings, the Social Democrats say that the energy tax relief recently touted by Chancellor Friedrich Merz "would have to be financed with additional debts.".

Ahead of Thursday's marathon talks, Merz had stated he hoped to introduce the tax relief amid the stress caused by issues including the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

The SPD's Dirk Wiese said the junior coalition partners were "not disinclined to pave the way for the electricity tax relief," but not by making cuts elsewhere.

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil of the SPD had stated he did not see enough fiscal wiggle room to enable the desired tax break.

Bremen's mayor Andreas Bovenshulte, also a Social Democrat, noted that while he would have welcomed the relief, other decisions meant it wasn't possible.

"For that, a serious financing source would have been required, for instance with a plastic or sugar of windfall tax," Bovenschulte remarked, in reference to either delayed or proposed but rejected plans to potentially increase tax revenues.

German defense industry startup Quantum Systems said its drones were operational worldwide once again, including with the Bundeswehr military, after a cyberattack by "hostile actors" last month.

The firm had confirmed the cyberattack on Thursday, amid reporting from the Financial Times that also stated the Bundeswehr had grounded its drones from the company.

"The fleet is operating normally around the globe — including Germany and the Bundeswehr," a Quantum Systems spokesperson noted in an emailed statement to the Reuters news agency. "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution.".

The tech giant, based near Munich, had earlier stated it uncovered an "active cyberattack" by hostile actors.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it stated in a statement, adding there was no risk for end people and operators using its unmanned systems.

Quantum drones are used by Ukrainian armed forces in their defensive war against Russia, among others.

It has been revealed that "Companies at the forefront of supporting Ukraine are being targeted precisely because our work is critically relevant to customers' security," the organization noted. "Being aware of this responsibility, Quantum Systems has mitigation intends in place and strives to fulfil the highest standard of data and system security.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Senior Christian Democrat Union (CDU) politician Matthias Middelberg appeared on ZDF television this morning to discuss the budget breakthrough.

He identified one "weak point" after the overnight negotiations.

"We have not yet saved enough, we still need to save a lot more," he stated.

Middelberg remarked that in his view the government would not be able to "collect the funds," because that would put too much tax strain on people and businesses.

Therefore, he mentioned, "the government must make cutbacks.".

Middelberg acepted that it wasn't clear how to do this, speculating that "perhaps there are subsidies or some other things" that could be ripe to be trimmed.

He stated the leadership of the coalition government's CDU/CSU and Social Democrats would "consider this question very closely once more.".

The German government statistics agency Destatis has published new figures on insolvency filings for the month of August.

A total of 2,067 companies registered insolvencies with German courts during the month, Destatis remarked, 4.4% more than in the same month in 2025.

The data operates on something of a delay, because the government tracks when courts grant the status, which can be almost three months after the initial application at times.

The increase has been a rolling trend this year. From January to August, 17,252 companies have filed for insolvency, 6.6% more than in the same period last year.

However, the total sum of debts forgiven in insolvency proceedings is actually quite considerably lower than in the first eight months of last year, at €25.9 billion ($28.7 billion) rather than €37.2 billion, because fewer large companies have gone bust.

Sources indicate that more individuals are also filing for bankruptcy protection than in 2025, although the rise is somewhat less sharp. In August, 6,301 people gained insolvency protection, 2.8% more than last August. For January through August, the year-on-year increase is more modest, at 1.2%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending intends for 2027 before the year's end.

Here are a few of the core statistics:.

Moin! Here's hoping you slept more and better than the Bundestag's budget committee. Or if not, at least let's hope that you had more fun.

Its members worked towards the dawn in a session lasting over 15 hours, trying to iron out the last wrinkles in spending intends for 2027.

The proverbial white smoke emerged at around 6 in the morning in Berlin, with word of a finalized agreement.

If you were tired of talk and criticism of the "debt brake" and the "black zero" (a promise not to take any new debts) in the years following the eurozone debt crisis, rest assured we can assign such chatter to the history books for now.

The borrowing looks for 2027 — if you incorporate new debt taken out as part of so-called "special funds," for instance for the military and infrastructure, rather than as part of the core budget — are the second highest in the history of post-war Germany.

The country only took out more newly introduced debt in 2021, at the height of the COVID pandemic and even then it was very close indeed.

We'll bring you more news and reactions on this, and whatever else breaks around the country, as Friday develops.

Kwame Brathwaite, photographer of 'Black is Beautiful' movement, dies at 85

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.
  • Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.
  • His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  This article was originally published by The Art Newspaper, an editorial partner of CNN Style.

Kwame Brathwaite, the pioneering activist and photographer whose work helped define the aesthetics of the “Black is Beautiful” movement of the 1960s and beyond, died on April 1, aged 85.

His son, Kwame Brathwaite, Jr, announced his father’s death in an Instagram post that read in part, “I am deeply saddened to share that my Baba, the patriarch of our family, our rock and my hero has transitioned.”.

Brathwaite’s work has been the subject of resurgent interest from curators, historians and collectors in recent years, and his first major institutional retrospective, which was organized by the Aperture Foundation, made its debut in 2019 at the Skirball Cultural Center in Los Angeles before touring the country.

Brathwaite was born in 1938 to Barbadian immigrants, in what he referred to as “the People’s Republic of Brooklyn” in Latest York, though his family moved from there to Harlem and then to the South Bronx when Brathwaite was 5 years old. He attended the School of Industrial Art (now the High School of Art and Design) and, according to profiles of Brathwaite in T Magazine and Vice, was drawn to photography by two moments. The first was in August of 1955, when a 17-year-old Brathwaite encountered David Jackson’s haunting photograph of a brutalized Emmett Till in his open casket. The second was in 1956, when — after he and his brother Elombe co-founded the African Jazz Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) — Brathwaite saw a young man taking photos in a dark jazz club without the use of a flash, and his mind became alight with possibility.

Sources indicate that using a Hasselblad medium-format camera, Brathwaite attempted to do the same, learning to work with limited light in a manner that enhanced the visual narrative of his imagery. He would soon also develop a darkroom technique that enriched and deepened how Black skin would appear in his photography, honing the practice in a small darkroom in his Harlem apartment. Brathwaite went on to photograph jazz legends performing throughout the 1950s and ’60s, including Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Thelonious Monk and others.

“You want to get the feeling, the mood that you’re experiencing when they’re playing,” Brathwaite told Aperture Magazine in 2017. “That’s the thing. You want to capture that.”.

A 106-year-old from the Philippines is Vogue's oldest ever cover model.

By the early 1960s, alongside the rest of AJASS, Brathwaite began using his photography and organizing prowess to consciously push back against whitewashed, Eurocentric beauty standards. The group came up with the concept of the Grandassa Models, young Black women whom Brathwaite would photograph, celebrating and accentuating their features. In 1962, AJASS organized “Naturally ’62”, a fashion show held in a Harlem club called the Purple Manor and featuring the models. The show would go on to be held regularly until 1992. In 1966, Brathwaite married his wife Sikolo, a Grandassa Model whom he had met on the street the year prior when he asked if he could take her portrait. The two remained married for the rest of Brathwaite’s life.

Sources indicate that by the 1970s, Brathwaite’s focus on jazz shifted to other forms of popular Black music. In 1974, he traveled to Africa with the Jackson Five to document their tour, also photographing the historic “Rumble in the Jungle” boxing match between Muhammad Ali and George Foreman in what’s now the Democratic Republic of Congo that same year. Commissions in this era also saw Brathwaite photographing Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder, Sly and the Family Stone, Bob Marley and other music legends.

Creating for community: The Black designers placing identity and heritage at the center of their brands.

According to recent reports, throughout the ensuing decades, Brathwaite continued to explore and develop his mode of photography, all through the lens of the “Black is Beautiful” ethos. In 2016, Brathwaite joined the roster of Philip Martin Gallery in Los Angeles, and he was continuing to photograph commissions as recently as 2018, when he shot artist and stylist Joanne Petit-Frère for The Fresh Yorker.

Recent findings suggest that T Magazine’s 2021 profile, published on the occasion of Brathwaite’s retrospective traveling to the Blanton Museum of Art in Austin, Texas, noted that the photographer’s health was failing such that he was unable to be interviewed for the article. A separate exhibition, “Kwame Brathwaite: Things Well Worth Waiting For,” is at the moment on view at the Art Institute of Chicago, where it will remain until July 24.

Sources indicate that “Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”.

A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

In a recent development, but if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

Sources indicate that but that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

By our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

In a recent development, the fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

According to recent reports, the next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In Fresh York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

Sources indicate that “Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”.

“The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”.

Recent findings suggest that peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”.

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

According to recent reports, martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I mentioned, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”.

With Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

“He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”.

One of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:.

Sources indicate that “There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ noted Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” says Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”.

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

It has been revealed that “Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

Industry observers note that “Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

Recent findings suggest that “Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

With Scott out of contract in 2028, the Cherries are under pressure to either extend his deal or sell him while they can still fetch a massive fee – but would rather not sell midseason, as they had to when Manchester City triggered Antoine Semenyo's release clause in January.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Co-hosted on home soil by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland, the road to Euro 2028 is fast approaching as the draw for qualifying takes place in Belfast in early December.

But the four co-hosts will enter qualifying for the tournament as normal, even though there is a ‘safety net’ that can be used by two of the teams should they fail to qualify automatically.

The United Kingdom hosted some games during the Covid-delayed Euro 2020 tournament in 2021, although many matches were played with limited capacities due to Covid restrictions.

Wembley hosted the final and will do so again in 2028, with Cardiff, Glasgow, Dublin, Birmingham, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle also staging games during the 24-team tournament.

Here’s everything you need to know ahead of the Euro 2028 qualifying draw, which takes place in Northern Ireland on Sunday 6 December.

Nations League play-offs: League A/B.

Nations League play-offs: League B/C.

In a recent development, unlike previous major tournaments held in multiple countries, England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland do not qualify automatically just because they are co-hosts. Although this is a tournament for the UK and Ireland, Northern Ireland are not considered co-hosts, as they are not staging any games.

But while England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland all enter qualifying as usual, there are two reserved places to be used by co-hosts if they fail to qualify automatically, either by winning their group or finishing as one of the eight-best runners-up.

The four co-hosts, as well as Northern Ireland for that matter, will all be kept apart in the qualifying draw to boost their qualification chances, so if they all go on to their win their groups then happy days – the safety net is not required.

But if disaster strikes and three or more of the co-hosts fail to qualify on merit, then there are just the two reserved places to fall back on: they will go to the two teams who have the best record in qualifying and the others will have to watch on.

The Euro 2028 qualifying draw takes place in Belfast on Sunday 6 December. Qualifying then begins in March 2027, but only for the teams not involved in the Nations League quarter-finals or Nations League play-offs who were drawn into Groups G-L. Within those groups of five, the four other teams will play against each other across March and June 2027, with everyone else then beginning their qualifying campaign from September 2027.

Published: 05:49 EST, 20 November 2026 | Updated: 08:12 EST, 20 November 2026.

A Liverpool fan accused of racially abusing footballer Antoine Semenyo has been found not guilty after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.

Semenyo was due to give evidence at Liverpool Magistrates' Court on Friday in the trial of Mark Mogan, 47, who was accused of shouting abuse during the opening match of the Premier League season at Anfield on August 15 last year.

But Simon Jones, prosecuting, said: 'Following recent contact made with Mr Semenyo, he has indicated he is no longer supportive of proceedings and the prosecution do not consider it is appropriate to compel him.

'In those circumstances we offer no further evidence in the case.' District Judge Mary Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty to the charge of racially aggravated behaviour.

Semenyo, who was a Bournemouth player at the time of the incident but later signed for Manchester City, had been due to give evidence last month but the trial was adjourned halfway through when Mr Mogan was taken to hospital after suffering a seizure.

The court had heard Mr Mogan, in a wheelchair, shouted at Semenyo as he went to take a throw-in about 30 minutes into the game.

Mark Mogan (right) has been found not guilty of racially abusing Antoine Semenyo (left) after the player withdrew his support for the prosecution.

He was alleged to have said: 'Hurry up and take the throw-in, you black b*****d.'.

Opening the case last month, Mr Jones said: 'That racial abuse was shouted directly at Antoine Semenyo, who was close to him.

'Mr Semenyo briefly froze, as he couldn't believe what the male had said.' Mr Mogan then shouted "I'm talking to you, you ****", the court heard.

Witnesses also mentioned they saw him throw his chewing gum at the footballer.

Semenyo reported the incident to the match referee and Mr Mogan was removed from the stadium at half-time.

Mr Mogan, who had an intermediary with him in court, told police in interview that Semenyo had called him a cripple after he shouted at the player to 'hurry up'.

Mr Mogan, of Templehill Close in Dovecot, Liverpool, declined to comment as he left court.

Semenyo, who scored a brace in the game, had brought the incident to the attention of match referee Anthony Taylor and the match was briefly halted while both managers and captains were spoken to.

At half time an announcement was made to the crowd asking for no racist abuse and pictures on social media demonstrated a man in a wheelchair being escorted along the touchline and out of the ground.

Mogan, pictured with Liverpool legend Robbie Fowler, would have been banned for life if he'd have been found guilty.

Merseyside Police later unveiled the man had been arrested and then was bailed for three months pending further investigations.

Pictures on social media showed Mogan playing wheelchair basketball for a team called the Greenbank Meteors while other images show him posing with Liverpool legends Robbie Fowler and Emile Heskey.

After he was charged, Liverpool confirmed he would be banned for life if found guilty but Judge Dowrick recorded a verdict of not guilty on Friday morning.
